doc.title: Herbie Hancock interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, November 18, 1995

title: Duets with Chick Corea and playing with Oscar Peterson
summary: The first rehearsals were cautious and polite, then became effortless; contrasted with playing with Oscar Peterson.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Yeah. I want to come in on one other thing. You know some people believe that the piano duets that you’ve done with Chick basically took pianistic virtuosity in terms of improvisation to its zenith. And some people said it hasn’t gone past that since.
Talk to us about the, you know, the two of you like spurring each other on, learning from each other, just like the virtuosity of the language, you know.

We — Chick and I — I should say about when we first got together to do the first tour, you know, when we first got together to rehearse, neither one of us had done anything quite like that before. He had done some duets I guess with his, well his then-girlfriend, now wife, Gayle Moran, who was working in his band and she’s also a singer. But there was sort of a different story because she hadn’t had the same kinds of experiences. She wasn’t like a heavyweight piano player per se, that wasn’t what she was about. Anyway Chick had two pianos in his house and — two big Steinways I guess they were or maybe a Bosendorfer and a Steinway concert grands — which was fortunate. That way we didn’t have to pay for a rehearsal studio and we didn’t have to rent pianos. It was great. And then we could just take our time and still really relax. But I was a little nervous about it and Chick was a little nervous about it too because we both really respected each other. You know we’re both contemporaries. And so we decided to take a tune, I don’t remember which tune it was, but we were both so cautious in the beginning. But it was funny to notice that that became easy. So then we would each start to take a few more chances. And that became easy. And then we started being less and less polite you know. Because at first we were so polite. You know I would play something and then I would wait to hear what Chick was going to play and really try to follow him you know, and leave him a lot of space. And he’d leave me space. It got to the point where we didn’t have to leave each other any space. We could both just play simultaneously and it didn’t even conflict. So we said, “Well, it looks like this is going to be a lot easier than we

thought.” It just happens that Chick and I just really fit each other. Somehow it just works. It’s amazing, you know, really amazing. I’ve had the great fortune also to play five concerts opposite Oscar Peterson but we played a couple of things together. So I mean that was a great opportunity for me. He’s one of the people that was a major influence on me when I was coming up. That’s a little more difficult, playing with Oscar. Maybe because he has been his own man for so long that he’s used to doing certain kinds of things and this is pretty far removed from what he’s accustomed to. But still, we were able to find a common ground and get something going. But with Chick it’s effortless. I don’t even have to think about him being, about providing a space for him you know. So it was really fantastic. And you’re right, we would feed each other constantly. I’ve got some stories I could tell you about some funny concerts. One time during the tour it became so easy to play together that we started trying to find other devices to use to kind of just a combination of either, like throwing a monkey wrench into the works just to give us something to deal with.
